title: Judar and His Brethren

full_text:
In Cairo lived an honest and pious young fisherman named Judar, whose two elder brothers, Salim and Salih, were envious, quarrelsome, and squandered their inheritance, repeatedly robbing Judar of his nets and clothes. Yet Judar never retaliated, sharing every fish he caught with his aged mother and forgiving his ungrateful brothers with saintly patience.

One day, while casting his net into the lake of Karun, Judar was approached by a mysterious Maghribi enchanter named Abd al-Samad. Recognizing Judar’s absolute purity of heart, the enchanter engaged him to retrieve the ancient talismanic treasure of King Shamhurish from an enchanted subterranean palace in the mountains of Fez.

Judar passed through seven terrifying halls of illusions—roaring dragons, enchanted swords, and phantom armies—by following the master’s advice: to keep his heart free from fear and his tongue engaged in prayer.

He retrieved the talismanic treasures: the magic saddlebag that produced whatever sumptuous food was desired; the golden ring that summoned an Ifrit; and the celestial scimitar that could rout armies.

Returning to Cairo, Judar used the magic saddlebag to feed all the poor and hungry of the city every day.

His jealous brothers, seeing his prosperity, betrayed him to the king’s corrupt vizier, who imprisoned Judar and seized the treasures.

Using the magic ring, Judar freed himself, overthrew the corrupt vizier, and was crowned King of Cairo by the joyful populace!

Instead of executing his treacherous brothers, Judar embraced them, appointed them emirs in his royal council, and shared his royal wealth with them, proving that boundless fraternal forgiveness is the truest crown of nobility.
moral: Pious patience, filial devotion, and endless fraternal forgiveness triumph over jealousy and treachery.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Judar and His Brethren"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
